edges.description: Losing either factor impairs biogenesis of the Q-, N- and PP-b-modules, through compromised integration of NDUFS3 and NDUFS5 and destabilisation of a third assembly factor, TIMMDC1. Forced NDUFAF4 expression rescues the Q-module defect caused by loss of NDUFAF3, which is direct evidence that the two act in one pathway with NDUFAF4 downstream or partly redundant.
edges.limitations: Drosophila, and no human variant is modelled - the manipulation is disruption of the fly orthologue, not knock-in of a patient allele. The module nomenclature also does not map cleanly: the fly work reports impaired Q-module biogenesis, whereas the human patient fibroblasts show Q-module subassemblies failing to form while P- and N-module intermediates accumulate. Both are consistent with NDUFAF4 acting at the Q-module, and neither settles which of the two readings of the human accumulation is right.

nodes.description:
A recommendation rather than a result, and it applies only to the optic-atrophy pole.
The 2026 series that found the NDUFAF4 optic-atrophy patients concludes that patients with nuclear complex I optic neuropathy may benefit from idebenone, dosed as for Leber hereditary optic neuropathy, where it is an approved therapy. Its rationale is mechanistic: reduced idebenone can bypass complex I and hand electrons from NADH directly to complex III, so any complex I defect might be partially corrected by it.
What the same paper reports about its own cohort is discouraging, and should be read alongside the recommendation: visual improvement was variable, with only three of thirteen patients showing some degree of response. Those thirteen are not thirteen NDUFAF4 patients - the sentence sits in a paragraph describing the whole thirty-one-patient series, directly after the list of drugs used, so the thirteen are most plausibly the patients who received idebenone. No response rate can be attributed to this genotype from it, and no individual NDUFAF4 patient's treatment or outcome is reported. Nothing at all has been reported for the severe pole, where an optic-nerve-directed therapy would not address the encephalopathy.

nodes.description:
A preclinical attempt at a gene-directed therapy. Recombinant NDUFAF4 was fused to the HIV TAT cell-penetrating peptide, expressed in E. coli, purified, and applied to fibroblasts from a patient in the founding family. The fusion protein reached the cells and their mitochondria, raised complex I activity and ATP production, increased cell number, and lowered reactive oxygen species.
It has never left cell culture. There is no animal work, no pharmacokinetics, no dosing and no trial - and the delivery problem this approach would have to solve in a patient is exactly the one cell culture does not test, since the affected organs are brain and optic nerve. It is curated because it is a real, published, mechanism-directed intervention for this specific gene, and because the alternative - listing nothing under treatments - would misrepresent the state of the field.
No therapeutic_agent is bound: no CHEBI or NCIT term names a TAT-NDUFAF4 fusion protein, and binding a term for something else would be worse than leaving the slot empty.
